name: Etruscan religion
info: Etruscan religion was the polytheistic belief and practice of the Etruscans of Etruria, in central Italy, from the Villanovan period; it is known for divination by entrails, thunder and lightning, and for a lost body of sacred books taken over by Rome.

facts.origin: Etruria, in the Villanovan culture; the earliest evidence for religious practices dates to the Villanovan period, including a 9th century BCE shrine at Tarquinia
facts.founder: none: the Etruscans believed their religion had been revealed to them by seers, chiefly Tages, a childlike figure born from tilled land, and the female figure Vegoia
facts.scriptures: none survive but the Liber Linteus, of about 800 surviving words; the Etrusca Disciplina, a corpus of sacred books, is known only from Roman writers
facts.followers: none: as the Etruscan civilisation was assimilated into the Roman Republic from the 4th century BCE its religion was absorbed into Roman culture, and knowledge of its language and religion soon ceased under the Julio-Claudians

t: The Etruscans believed their religion had been revealed to them by seers, chiefly Tages and Vegoia, and consulted the gods through signs, divination by animal entrails, thunder and lightning.
No Etruscan sacred text survives except the Liber Linteus; the Etrusca Disciplina, a corpus of sacred books, is known only through Roman writers such as Cicero and Valerius Maximus.
Roman haruspices and noble families claiming Etruscan descent carried the religion into Roman public life long after the people of Etruria had forgotten the language.

sections.origins:
The earliest evidence for Etruscan religious practices dates to the Villanovan period, and the first attestations of an Etruscan religion are traced to the Villanovan culture. Sites such as the 9th century BCE shrine at Pian d’Civita in Tarquinia and Veii’s Piazza d’Armi grew into fully developed sanctuaries, and cemeteries of the period show cremation burial in urns with grave goods. By the 6th century BCE Etruscan sanctuaries had become increasingly monumental, with major temples, expensive offerings and evidence for animal sacrifice and other rituals.

The Etruscans were polytheistic. Their mythology shows some syncretism with Greek and Roman traditions, yet the conception and worship of their divinities was individual and not an adoption of other cultures’ practices. In the Archaic period Greek settlers and traders interacted with Italic communities along the central Mediterranean coasts and brought their mythological narratives. It is unclear how much figures such as Hercle (Heracles) or Menvra (Minerva) derived from the Greeks, and to what degree they already existed among some Italian communities.

Greek claims that the sons of Odysseus had once ruled over the Etruscans date to at least the mid-6th century BCE, and Lycophron and Theopompus link Odysseus to Cortona, where he was called Nanos. Linking an origin to a Greek hero could give non-Greek groups an advantage over rivals in Italy. Whether Odysseus served the Etruscans as the heroic leader who led them to settle their lands cannot be proven at present.
sections.beliefs:
The Etruscans believed in intimate contact with divinity and did nothing without consulting the gods and seeking signs from them. They seem to have held that deities could be negotiated with through sacrifices and celestial observation. A god was called an ais, later eis, and a sacred place such as a grave or temple was a fanu or luth, where a worshipper would make a fler, an offering. The Liber Linteus appears to distinguish gods of light from gods of darkness.

Three layers of deities appear in Etruscan art. One seems to be of indigenous origin: Usil, god or goddess of the sun, Tivr of the moon, Turan, goddess of love, Laran, god of war, Selvans, god of the woods, Turms, messenger of the gods, Fufluns, god of wine, and underworld deities such as Catha and Lur. Above them stood higher deities that seem to reflect the Indo-European system: Tin or Tinia, the sky, his wife Uni, Nethuns, god of the waters, and Cel, the earth goddess. Greek gods and heroes were adopted during the Orientalizing Period, and over time the primary trinity became Tinia, Uni and Menrva, venerated in tripartite temples similar to the later Roman Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. The dii involuti, the “veiled gods”, are sometimes said to be superior to all others, but were never worshipped, named or depicted directly.

The gods were closely tied to places in the landscape. Sanctuaries often stood near physical features, and the boundaries between water and land, and between earth and sky, were considered sacred; some sanctuaries near water sources were used from the Bronze Age.
sections.texts:
No Etruscan sacred text survives except the Liber Linteus, found wrapped around the Zagreb mummy. Only about 800 words survive, and it appears to be a brontoscopic calendar describing ritual activities. Roman authors, including Livy, Cicero and Varro, frequently refer to the Etrusca Disciplina, supposedly a collection of sacred books that gave instructions for communicating with the gods through natural signs, haruspicy and augury. The name appears in Valerius Maximus, and Cicero refers to a disciplina.

Massimo Pallottino summarises what is known from other sources about the corpus. The revelations of the prophet Tages, the Libri Tagetici, included the rules of divination from animal entrails and discussion of the afterlife and its rituals, the Libri Acherontici. The revelations of the prophetess Vegoia, the Libri Vegoici, included divination from thunder and from lightning strikes, the Libri Fulgurales. Books on omens and prodigies and books on fate detailed the proper ways to found cities, erect shrines, drain fields, formulate laws and measure space and time.

Pallottino calls the Etrusca Disciplina a religious and political “constitution”: it does not dictate what laws shall be made or how people are to behave, but sets rules for asking the gods questions and receiving answers. Publius Nigidius Figulus, a contemporary of Varro, made a Latin translation of the brontoscopic calendar of Tages, which survives in a Byzantine Greek manuscript. Etruscan mythology is also evidenced by pottery, architectural terracottas, inscriptions, engraved mirrors and votive objects.
sections.spread:
Etruscan religion belonged to the lands of Etruria, and its history is one of contact and absorption. The Etruscans adopted gods from other religions, integrating them as important cult deities and adapting their names and aspects of their powers; they took the deities Juno, Minerva and Neptunus as Uni, Menrua and Nethuns. During the Orientalizing Period of 750/700–600 BCE Greek gods and heroes such as Aritimi (Artemis), Hercle and Pacha (Bacchus) entered the Etruscan system. The Etruscans, the Romans and other native Italic peoples all influenced one another’s beliefs and practices.

After the Etruscan defeat in the Roman–Etruscan Wars in 264 BCE, the remaining Etruscan culture began to be assimilated into the Roman. The Roman Senate adopted key elements of the Etruscan religion, and the Romans took over the practices of consulting signs in total, adopting the practice of haruspicy. These elements were perpetuated by haruspices and by noble Roman families who claimed Etruscan descent, long after the general population of Etruria had forgotten the language.

In the last years of the Roman Republic the religion began to fall out of favour and was satirised by public figures such as Cicero. The Julio-Claudians, especially Claudius, whose first wife, Plautia Urgulanilla, claimed Etruscan descent, kept some knowledge of the language and religion for a short time longer, but the practice soon ceased.
sections.community:
The Etruscans seem to have had specific religious personnel. Divinatory inquiries were conducted by priests whom the Romans called haruspices or sacerdotes, and Tarquinii had a college of 60 of them. Inscriptions use several words for religious officials, among them capen, maru, eisnev and hatrencu, the last for a priestess, and the Etruscans called the art of haruspicy ziχ neθsrac. Votives in bronze and terracotta show how different groups worshipped; they were often inscribed with the name of the deity.

Women in Etruria had more social liberties than Roman women until the Roman absorption of Etruria. Husband and wife often stood side by side in representations, and women appear on sarcophagi at the same ceremonial feasts as men. Women’s votives included statuettes, items related to textile production such as spindle whorls, and anatomical votives including wombs; inscriptions by women are about one sixth of the votive inscriptions. Whether the hatrencu was a priestess is widely debated: many scholars say the unusual burial of a group of women at Vulci and the obscure term point to one, while others disagree, and whether there were female religious specialists in Etruria is mainly speculation.

Etruscan tombs imitated domestic structures, with spacious chambers, wall paintings and grave furniture. The deceased was shown on the sarcophagus in their prime, often with a spouse, and cremation and inhumation were both practised. The underworld was patterned after the Greek Hades, ruled by Aita, with the dead guided there by the blue, hammer-wielding Charun.
sections.legacy:
Etruscan religion survived chiefly through Rome. The Roman Senate adopted key elements of it, and haruspicy passed to the Romans, while the Etruscans had taken Juno, Minerva and Neptunus as Uni, Menrua and Nethuns. Etruscan beliefs and mythologies were often incorporated into Roman culture, following the Roman tendency to absorb the local gods and customs of other peoples. The tripartite temples of Tinia, Uni and Menrva resemble the later Roman Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus.

Because no Etruscan sacred text survives except the Liber Linteus, it is impossible to understand the religion fully, and what is known comes from archaeology and from Roman writers. Altars, animal bones in sanctuaries and cemeteries, votive objects, inscriptions and engraved mirrors give insight into practice. The Etruscan inscriptions have been presented by Helmut Rix in Etruskische Texte and analysed linguistically by Rex Wallace in Zikh Rasna, and a catalogue of mythological figures is held in the Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae.

The Etruscans’ own beliefs remain open to interpretation. Scholars still debate whether Hercle and Menvra were largely Greek in origin, and whether Odysseus served as a leader for the Etruscans.

summary: Etruscan religion was the polytheistic belief and practice of the Etruscans of central Italy, from the Villanovan period. It centred on seers’ revelations, sacred books and divination by entrails, thunder and lightning, and is known only from archaeology and Roman writers. After the defeat of 264 BCE it was absorbed into Roman religion through the haruspices.
notes: Dates: start -900 circa from the 9th century BCE shrine at Tarquinia and 'the first attestations ... can be traced back to the Villanovan culture'. End 100 circa is my choice: the article gives no end year, only that the Julio-Claudians kept knowledge 'for a short time longer, but this practice soon ceased', and dates the Piacenza liver to the 1st or 2nd century CE. Change it if a different end is preferred.

Event '8th century BCE': the article gives the Orientalizing Period as '750/700–600 BC'; I placed it in the 8th century as the earlier figure. Event '525 BCE' is the start of the article's 525–500 BCE range for the Orvieto statue base.

Contradiction left out: the Gravisca kylix is dated 'late fourth or early fifth century BCE' in the article, and I did not use it. The article spells 'Veogia' once and 'Vegoia' elsewhere; I used Vegoia. 'Menvra' appears once; kept as written for Hercle and Menvra in origins. 'Pian d'Civita' is the article's spelling.

Left out: Poggio Colla textile finds (speculative), the Hinthial, Tuchulcha and the Tabulae Iguvinae (Umbrian), the Herios festival and Semele passage (obscure in the article), Roman-era assertions about the Julio-Claudians beyond Claudius.

The people are known through Roman writers (Livy, Cicero, Varro, Valerius Maximus), Greek authors and archaeology; this is said in the sections. References are left empty for the editor; the article's bibliography includes De Grummond and Simon (eds), The Religion of the Etruscans (2006), Jannot, Religion in Ancient Etruria (2005), Pallottino, The Etruscans (1975).

Faith map: Etruria is level 2 until 264 BCE and level 1 after, as the religion was absorbed; Rome is level 1 from 264 BCE as the Senate adopted its elements. No 'last' mark: the article names no last place. Coordinates are general geography for named places.
